overview: Both synthesise nucleic acid chains from a DNA template, but they build different products and have different accuracy requirements.
genZNote: DNA polymerase double-checks every word it writes. RNA polymerase just writes fast and moves on.

aspects.label: Primer Requirement
aspects.valueA: Requires a short RNA primer to begin synthesis.
aspects.valueB: Does not require a primer — can initiate synthesis on its own.

aspects.label: Proofreading Ability
aspects.valueA: Has 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity, giving very high fidelity.
aspects.valueB: Generally lacks proofreading activity, making it more error-prone.

aspects.label: Synthesis Direction
aspects.valueA: Synthesises in the 5' to 3' direction, reading the template 3' to 5'.
aspects.valueB: Also synthesises in the 5' to 3' direction, reading the template 3' to 5'.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: DNA polymerase's need for a primer is exactly why lagging strand synthesis requires repeated RNA primers and Okazaki fragments.
overlay.memoryTrick: DNA polymerase = precise editor. RNA polymerase = fast first-drafter.
overlay.commonMisconception: RNA polymerase's lower fidelity isn't a design flaw — RNA is short-lived and made in many copies, so occasional errors matter less than in DNA.
